props.title: Frances

sections.content: Frances (1982) stands as one of Hollywood's most harrowing portraits of mental illness and the brutal treatment of women in the studio system. Jessica Lange delivers a tour-de-force performance as Frances Farmer, the rebellious 1930s actress whose outspoken nature and refusal to conform led to forced institutionalization. The film pairs powerfully with One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (1975) in its depiction of psychiatric abuse, while echoing the tragic Hollywood descents shown in Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Whatever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962).

sections.content: The film's unflinching look at psychiatric treatment in mid-20th century America connects to a larger cinematic examination of institutional power and medical abuse. The Snake Pit (1948) broke ground in depicting mental health treatment, while later films like A Beautiful Mind (2001) and Shutter Island (2010) continued exploring the complex relationship between mental illness, treatment, and social control. Lange's raw performance particularly resonates with other actresses portraying real-life figures who faced similar struggles, like Natalie Portman in Jackie (2016). SUBHEAD: Hollywood's Dark Mirror

Frances serves as a crucial critique of Hollywood's star system and its destruction of female talent. The film pairs naturally with Mulholland Drive (2001) and Star 80 (1983) in exposing the industry's exploitation of women. Director Graeme Clifford captures both the glamour and grotesque reality of the studio era, while showing how Farmer's independence and intellectual pursuits marked her as a threat to the patriarchal system. Her story prefigures later examinations of Hollywood abuse like An Open Secret (2014).
